name: Analytical Chemistry
tagline: Precision instrumentation and advanced methods for molecular characterization.
seo_title: Analytical Chemistry — paper summaries, news & innovations | Chemisters
seo_description: Follow Chemisters Analytical Chemistry on LinkedIn and Facebook: paper summaries, news and innovations in chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy and sensors.

definition.lead: Analytical chemistry answers two questions about any sample: what is in it, and how much.
definition.body: It provides the methods every other field depends on, from the glucose meter and the doping test to the spectrum that confirms a new drug's structure. A good method is judged by three words: accurate, precise and sensitive.

facts.label: core questions: what is in a sample, and how much of it
Mikhail Tsvet coins 'chromatography' after separating plant pigments
gas chromatography is introduced by James and Martin

branches.name: Chromatography
branches.summary: Separating mixtures by how strongly each component sticks to a stationary phase.
branches.example: HPLC checks the purity of almost every medicine.

branches.name: Mass spectrometry
branches.summary: Weighing molecules as ions to identify them.
branches.example: Doping tests and protein analysis rely on it.

branches.name: UV–visible & IR spectroscopy
branches.summary: Identifying and measuring substances through the light they absorb.
branches.example: The Beer–Lambert law turns absorbance into concentration.

branches.name: NMR spectroscopy
branches.summary: Nuclear spins in a magnetic field reveal how atoms are connected.
branches.example: The standard way to confirm a newly made molecule.

branches.name: Electroanalysis
branches.summary: Measuring with electrodes: pH, ions, glucose.
branches.example: Blood glucose meters are electrochemical sensors.

branches.name: Classical analysis
branches.summary: Titration and weighing: measuring by reacting with a known amount.
branches.example: Acid–base titrations are still used in quality labs.

branches.name: Quality control
branches.summary: Proving that products meet their specifications.
branches.example: Every medicine batch is tested before release.

branches.name: Forensic & environmental analysis
branches.summary: Finding traces in evidence and in the environment.
branches.example: Detecting pesticide residues in drinking water.

timeline.title: Beer's law
timeline.text: August Beer relates how much light a solution absorbs to its concentration.
timeline.why: The basis of every spectrophotometric measurement.

timeline.title: Spectroscopy finds new elements
timeline.text: Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff discover caesium from its spectral lines.
timeline.why: Showed that light can identify elements.

timeline.title: Chromatography is named
timeline.text: Mikhail Tsvet separates plant pigments into coloured bands and calls it chromatography.
timeline.why: The ancestor of every separation method used today.

timeline.title: The pH scale
timeline.text: Søren Sørensen introduces pH while studying proteins at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen.
timeline.why: A single number for acidity, used everywhere.

timeline.title: Early mass spectrometry
timeline.text: J. J. Thomson separates two isotopes of neon by their mass.
timeline.why: The first step toward weighing molecules.

timeline.title: Polarography
timeline.text: Jaroslav Heyrovský invents polarography with a dropping mercury electrode.
timeline.why: Launched modern electroanalysis; Nobel Prize in 1959.

timeline.title: NMR is observed
timeline.text: Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell independently detect nuclear magnetic resonance in matter.
timeline.why: Became chemistry's most powerful structure tool; Nobel Prize in 1952.

timeline.title: Gas chromatography
timeline.text: Anthony James and Archer Martin introduce gas–liquid chromatography.
timeline.why: Made the analysis of volatile mixtures fast and routine.

timeline.title: Big molecules fly
timeline.text: Nobel Prize to John Fenn and Koichi Tanaka for soft ionization of biomolecules, shared with Kurt Wüthrich for protein NMR.
timeline.why: Proteins can now be weighed intact by mass spectrometry.

quiz.q: A method gives 10.1, 10.2 and 10.1 for a true value of 12.0. It is…
quiz.explain: The results agree closely with each other (precise) but sit far from the true value (not accurate).

quiz.q: The Beer–Lambert law relates absorbance to…
quiz.explain: A = εlc: absorbance grows with concentration and the distance light travels through the sample.

quiz.q: In a mass spectrometer, ions are separated by their…
quiz.explain: Electric and magnetic fields steer ions according to m/z.
In 1906 Tsvet separated plant pigments into coloured bands. 'Chroma' means colour.

quiz.q: How many times more H⁺ is in a solution at pH 3 than at pH 5?
quiz.explain: pH is logarithmic: each unit is a factor of 10, so two units is 10 × 10.

quiz.q: In reversed-phase HPLC, which compound usually comes out first?
quiz.explain: The stationary phase is non-polar (C18), so polar compounds interact least and elute first.

quiz.q: Which technique best shows which atoms are bonded to which in an organic molecule?
quiz.explain: NMR reveals each atom's environment and its neighbours through couplings.

quiz.q: In a flame test, sodium colours the flame…
quiz.explain: Excited sodium atoms emit strongly at about 589 nm, the yellow of old street lamps.

quiz.q: Why add an internal standard to a sample?
options: To correct for losses and instrument variation
To give the sample a colour the detector can see
To raise the sample's mass above the detection limit
To sterilize the sample before it enters the instrument
quiz.explain: Measuring the analyte relative to a known added compound cancels many sources of error.

options: The smallest amount reliably distinguished from a blank
quiz.explain: Below it, a signal cannot be told apart from noise.

quiz.q: The 2002 Nobel Prize for soft ionization of biomolecules went to…
quiz.explain: Their methods (electrospray and soft laser desorption) let intact proteins be weighed. Kurt Wüthrich shared the prize for protein NMR.

options: Current while sweeping voltage at a mercury electrode
quiz.explain: Each reducible species gives a step in current at its own potential.
